action_statement: I always stand up and greet every patient and their guardian with a smile
description: Stand, smile, make eye contact. That moment says: “We’re glad you’re here.” It costs nothing and changes everything.
intervention_text: Standing up commands respect and shows warmth. If your legs are tired, at least lean forward and make direct eye contact. Do not greet the computer screen.

action_statement: I always check for a complete medical history and required forms for the visit before changing patient status to either "Checked In" OR "Arrived - No Paperwork
description: Don’t mark them “checked in” until the forms are done. It protects the clinical team’s time and keeps the visit running clean.
intervention_text: A checked box protects a life. Never auto-pilot this. If the form isn't signed, the patient isn't Ready. Hold the line.

action_statement: I always fully complete the check in process with an offer of hospitality and introduction to the play area before returning to other tasks.
description: Greet, welcome, and finish the moment. Hospitality first, multitasking second, it’s how families know they matter here.
intervention_text: Don't leave them hanging. The Play Area Handoff is the period at the end of the sentence. Practice transitioning from paperwork to welcome today.

action_statement: I always actively alert the clinical team that a patient is ready to be pulled back directly after changing patient status to "Checked In
description: The second you hit “Checked In,” tell the back. It’s a small habit that keeps patients moving and the day flowing.
intervention_text: The baton pass matters. If you click Checked In but don't tell the back, the baton hits the floor. Walk back there or use the chat immediately.

action_statement: I always tidy the reception area, check the patient bathroom, and restock amenities in the front area once every hour.
description: Keep the front fresh. A quick reset each hour shows pride in your space and helps every family feel like the first one of the day.
intervention_text: You get used to the mess. Reset your eyes. Walk out the front door and walk back in. What is the first thing you notice? Fix it.

action_statement: I always examine the schedule two days ahead and first call, then send a personalized text message until all unconfirmed appointments are confirmed.
description: Two days ahead is the sweet spot. A quick call, then a personalized text, keeps the schedule full and should help you feel some peace of mind.
intervention_text: This is the sweet spot. If you are calling day-of, you are already behind. Pull the 2 Days Out list today and make 5 calls.

action_statement: I always review patient memos and appointment notes prior to beginning the check in process
description: Read the notes before the hello. You’ll greet each family with context, confidence, and fewer surprises.
intervention_text: Being able to reference individual situations with grace takes your service up a notch. Check the memo for Anxiety or Billing Issues before you say hello. It prevents awkward surprises and puts you one step ahead.

action_statement: I always ask guardians what their goals are for the visit and enter the answer into appointment notes before booking a new appointment
description: Taking time to ask about goals tells families you’re on their side. It’s not just small talk, it’s how trust begins.

action_statement: I always dedicate time daily to call and send a personalized text to people on the short call list, prioritizing same-day or next-day open treatment slots.
description: Fill the day, but keep it personal. A short, genuine call or text makes families feel remembered, not marketed to, and helps more kids get care faster.
intervention_text: An empty chair is a missed opportunity. Ask the Office Manager to show you exactly how to filter the ASAP List in the software so you aren't guessing who to call.

action_statement: I am able to name all common procedures and their typical duration from memory
description: Know the basics cold. When you can answer confidently, families trust you and scheduling stays accurate and stress-free.
intervention_text: Confidence comes from knowing the details. Pick one procedure you felt unsure about today and ask a Lead to explain the basic steps to you in 2 minutes.

action_statement: I always communicate our office's NPO guidelines for all relevant appointments when confirming
description: If patient's haven't followed proper NPO guidelines, their appointment could need to be rescheduled. You're their last reminder to get that right.
intervention_text: Safety is non-negotiable. If you are fuzzy on the NPO rules, pull up the Pre-Op Checklist right now. Better to double-check than risk a rescheduled surgery.

action_statement: I always communicate the importance of X-rays to our standard of care any time a parent objects or attempts to decline them.
description: Parents hesitate because they care. You bridge that moment by calmly explaining that X-rays protect their child’s health, helping them see care, not cost.
intervention_text: Parents decline when they don't see value. Practice this line: X-rays let us see what our eyes can't. Ask a Lead to hear you say it to ensure you sound confident, not pushy.

action_statement: When presented with critical feedback, I always remain calm and first restate the guardian's feedback
description: Take a breath before you speak. Restate what you heard to show you understand, it turns feedback from a hit to a handshake.
intervention_text: Validation lowers the temperature. Practice saying: I want to make sure I hear you correctly. You're saying [X]? Ask a Lead to roleplay this with you for 60 seconds.

action_statement: I always preview the patient's doctor by name, and comment specifically on that doctor's expertise or experience when scheduling an appointment
description: Drop the doctor’s name and one genuine detail about their skill. It makes families feel secure and reminds them they’re in good hands.
intervention_text: Building the doctor up builds the parent's confidence. Pick one specific strength for each doctor today (e.g., Great with anxiety) and use it in your next scheduling call.

action_statement: I always inform the guardian about completing paperwork via the patient portal when scheduling or confirming appointments.
description: Give them a head start. A quick reminder about the portal saves time at check-in and makes the visit feel effortless for everyone.
intervention_text: Front-loading paperwork saves everyone's sanity. Ask a Lead to show you the Portal Status view so you can spot missing forms before the patient walks in.

action_statement: I always notify the practice manager then Lead RDA immediately if a patient has been "Checked In" and waiting for longer than 10 minutes
description: When wait times stretch, act fast. Loop in the right people early to solve the problem before it becomes one.
intervention_text: Silence feels like indifference to a waiting parent. You are the alarm. Ask the Practice Manager today: How do you prefer I alert you when we hit the Red Zone?

action_statement: I always firmly and kindly inform 48-hr cancellations or reschedules of their consequence level, and the next consequence, before offering one last opportunity to keep the appointment.
description: Policies protect the schedule, but empathy protects relationships. Explain clearly, stay kind, and end with one last chance to keep the appointment.
intervention_text: Tone is everything here. You want Firm Kindness. Read the specific Cancellation Policy script out loud twice before your next call to lock in the verbiage.

action_statement: I always use gloves only when handling contaminated instruments or chemicals, and remove them before touching anything clean or sterile.
description: Clean and sterile items stay safe when you use gloves only for what’s dirty. This habit prevents cross-contamination and protects both patients and the clinical team.
intervention_text: Cross-contamination happens when we rush. Pause right now and visualize your Clean to Dirty flow. Ask a Lead RDA to audit your next room turnover.

action_statement: I always greet the patient by name, smile with eye contact, and introduce myself by name.
description: The first moments set the tone. A warm greeting with eye contact helps the child feel safe and helps parents relax, knowing you’re attentive and present.
intervention_text: A name is a safety signal. Look at the chart, say the name out loud to yourself, then go get the patient. Make eye contact immediately.

action_statement: I always check the patient memo and ensure a complete medical history before beginning the appointment
description: Reviewing memos and history before you start keeps everyone safe and prevents surprises. It helps you walk into the room prepared and confident.
intervention_text: Never fly blind. Read the Medical Alerts out loud to yourself before the patient sits down. If something looks odd, ask the Doctor.

action_statement: I always tell, show, do before performing any action on a patient.
description: Kids feel safer when they know what’s coming. Showing and explaining each step builds trust, reduces fear, and helps the visit go smoothly.
intervention_text: Surprise equals fear. Never touch without talking. Practice your Tell script for the suction straw: It's just a thirsty straw that makes a slurping sound.

action_statement: I always immediately change patient status to "In Chair" when they are seated and "Treatment Complete" when they are ready to be checked out.
description: Updating status right away keeps the whole team coordinated. It helps the doctor see who’s ready and keeps families from waiting longer than necessary.
intervention_text: The status runs the board. If you don't click In Chair, the front desk thinks the room is empty. Update it the second they sit down.

action_statement: I always take a moment to assess the parent’s and patient’s mood after changing status to ‘In Chair,’ and I quietly share any concerns with the doctor.
description: Reading the room early helps the doctor understand what kind of visit it may be. Quietly passing along concerns allows the doctor to adjust their approach with care and sensitivity.
intervention_text: Read the room. If the parent looks anxious, whisper a heads-up to the Doctor before they enter. It helps them adjust their entry energy.

action_statement: I always verify that my Xrays are usable for the doctor before moving the patient from the Xray machine
description: Checking the image right away saves time and prevents repeat exposures. Ensuring clarity helps the doctor diagnose accurately and keeps the visit moving.
intervention_text: Don't guess on shadows. If the apex isn't clear, retake it immediately. A bad X-ray wastes the Doctor's time during the exam.

action_statement: I check Uptime and complete outstanding tasks prior to departure every day
description: Finishing Uptime tasks daily keeps the practice safe, compliant, and ready for the next day. Consistent follow-through prevents surprises and protects patient care.
intervention_text: Don't leave it for the closer. If you have 5 minutes, wipe a counter or stock a drawer. Small acts now prevent late nights later.

action_statement: If I help explain a treatment plan, I always ask the parent "How does that sound to you?" or "How are you feeling about this plan?".
description: A gentle check-in helps parents feel heard and reassured. Asking how the plan feels opens the door for real questions before they become concerns.

action_statement: I always ask the doctor to review my charting for accuracy before the doctor leaves the chair.
description: A quick accuracy check prevents rework later. Confirming while the doctor is still present keeps charting clean, complete, and reliable.
intervention_text: Accuracy is a team sport. Before the Doctor leaves, ask: Just to confirm, we did DO on 3 and 14, correct? Catch the error now, not at billing.

action_statement: I always verify that proper consent forms have been completed prior to beginning the appointment
description: Confirming consents protects both the patient and the practice. A quick check at the start ensures care begins safely and legally.
intervention_text: No consent, no treatment. If the signature is missing, do not recline the chair. Ask the parent to sign on the iPad immediately.

action_statement: After scheduling the next appointment, I always verbally emphasize the importance keeping that appointment and the consequences for missing it.
description: A brief reminder sets expectations early. Emphasizing the importance helps families commit to care and prevents unnecessary delays in treatment.

action_statement: When a parent is uncertain about a procedure, I always reassure them about the importance of the procedure, and inform the doctor about the conversation
description: Parents worry because they care. Offering calm reassurance and looping in the doctor keeps communication clear and helps families feel supported.
intervention_text: Validate, don't argue. Say: It makes sense that you are worried about [X]. Here is why we recommend it... Connect it to safety.

action_statement: When responding to frustration, I always remain calm and first attempt to restate the guardian's complaint.
description: Starting with calmness keeps tough conversations productive. Restating what you heard shows that you’re listening and takes the tension out of the moment.

action_statement: I always preview the patient's doctor by name, and comment specifically on that doctor's expertise or experience
description: Introducing the doctor with a quick note about their skill builds instant confidence. It helps parents feel at ease before the doctor even enters the room.
intervention_text: Sell the expert. Dr. Jones is amazing at these fillings. Transfer your trust to the parent.

action_statement: When confirming next steps, I always highlight the health risks of delaying treatment or recare.
description: Delays can create real risks, and parents appreciate honesty delivered with care. Explaining those risks clearly helps them make informed, confident decisions.
intervention_text: This can be a gentle but firm reality check. You've seen what happens when treatment is delayed. Tell them kindly.

action_statement: I always genuinely offer coffee or water to guardians after check in is complete
description: Offer something simple, a coffee, a water, a smile. Those few seconds turn a transaction into a welcome
intervention_text: Hospitality disrupts anxiety. If you feel too busy to offer water, you are too busy. Pause, breathe, and make the offer.

action_statement: I always confirm insurance verification status prior to completing check-in.
description: Confirm insurance before you close the chart. It saves headaches later and tells families you’ve already handled the details.
intervention_text: Verification is the gatekeeper. If you aren't sure if a plan is active, ask the Insurance Coordinator to verify it with you right now.

action_statement: I always answer phones within 3 rings, respond to texts within 3 minutes, and return emails within 3 hours.
description: Fast replies build confidence. When families know you’re responsive, they stop worrying if anyone’s paying attention.
intervention_text: Responsiveness is our brand. If you are missing these targets, you might be multitasking too much. Ask a colleague to watch your workflow for 10 mins and help spot the bottleneck.

action_statement: I always thoroughly vaccuum the front area in the morning, before leaving for lunch, and at the end of the day.
description: Every detail families see tells a story. A spotless front area says, “we care about our space, and about you.”
intervention_text: A clean floor signals a clean clinic. If this slips, check your Closing Checklist routine. Do you need to start 10 minutes earlier?

action_statement: I always communicate the importance of attendance and ask whether we can count on them to be there when booking any appointment.
description: Turn confirmation into partnership. Framing it as “can we count on you?” builds respect and accountability without pressure.
intervention_text: Can we count on you? is a psychological hook. If you feel awkward saying it, roleplay it with a peer today until it feels like a natural part of the conversation.

action_statement: I always inform the clinical team of existing or anticipated patient balance using the info board.
description: Keep everyone in the loop. A quick note on the board prevents confusion, smooths handoffs, and helps families feel every detail’s handled.
intervention_text: The Board helps keep all of us on track. If you forget to write on it it, the clinical team can miss crucial information. Set a mental trigger: Check-in isn't done until the Board is written.

action_statement: I always call the guardian and patient by their preferred name (not kiddo or mom)
description: Names are powerful. Using them turns routine interactions into real connection, small word, big signal of respect.

action_statement: If we are running more than 10 minutes behind schedule, I always gently communicate that to the families in my waiting room one at a time, and assure them that we are working diligently to catch up.
description: A short, sincere update matters more than a perfect schedule. Let families know you see the delay, you care, and you’re working to make it right.
intervention_text: Ignoring a delay makes it worse. Go into the lobby right now and give a 30-second update to anyone waiting. I see you, and we're hurrying goes a long way.

action_statement: I am able to list the procedures that are most commonly denied by each insurance
description: Understand what insurance often pushes back on, it keeps conversations honest. Setting clear expectations early builds trust fast.
intervention_text: Don't let insurance surprises hurt the patient relationship. Review the Common Denials cheat sheet with the Office Manager so you can warn parents upfront.

action_statement: I am able to calmly and confidently provide aftercare instructions for all common procedures.
description: Speak like you’ve done it a hundred times. Calm, clear aftercare makes families feel safe, confident, and cared for long after they leave.
intervention_text: You are the final voice of care. Read the Aftercare Script for fillings out loud. If you stumble, practice it one more time. Clarity prevents callbacks.

action_statement: I always explain that having insurance info up front will contribute to a smooth visit, and I offer to wait while families gather that information.
description: We want to take every opportunity to gather our clerical requirements. A little extra time up front saves us from scrambling or rushing when they're with us in person
intervention_text: It's not about money; it's about a smooth visit. Try saying: I want to make sure you don't get stuck with a bill later. It frames the request as a favor to them.

action_statement: When presented with critical feedback, I actively acknowledge my personal or our collective role in the situation.
description: Teams grow when people own their part. Admit what’s true, skip the spin, and help fix it fast.
intervention_text: Defensiveness kills trust. Try the Two Words ownership trick: I apologize. Ask the Office Manager how they handle valid complaints without over-promising.

action_statement: I am able to list the innovative technologies, materials, and processes our practice uses and explain how they lead to positive health outcomes.
description: Families love hearing what makes your office stand out. Share it with pride, your confidence helps them trust the quality of care.
intervention_text: You don't need to be an engineer, just a fan. Ask a Lead: What is one cool thing about our laser/scanner that I can tell parents? Use that fact today.

action_statement: I always verbally preview the excellent service to expect during an exceptional visit when booking an appointment.
description: Give them a glimpse of what’s ahead. A confident preview sets high expectations and shows that great service is standard here.
intervention_text: Set the stage. Saying You're going to love Dr. Smith creates a placebo effect of a good visit. Say it to the next patient you book.

action_statement: When two or more families arrive within 3 minutes, I always note arrival order and suggest a pull order to the clinical team (“A then B”) using the tablets to keep the lobby moving.
intervention_text: You are the air traffic controller. Don't just check them in; sequence them. Explicitly tell the back: Family A arrived first, please seat them before Family B.

action_statement: I always inform patients of outstanding balances during appointment confirmation preparing them for that balance to be collected at check in.
description: Be upfront before they arrive. Transparency turns a potential awkward moment into one of trust and professionalism.
intervention_text: Money conversations are hard but necessary. Don't surprise them at the desk. Practice the Pre-Call script: Just a heads up on that balance... so they arrive prepared.

action_statement: I always set up the tray for the scheduled procedure and any likely alternatives before bringing the patient back.
description: Preparing the full tray in advance keeps appointments smooth and prevents scrambling once the patient is seated. It creates confidence for the doctor, the patient, and for you.
intervention_text: Scrambling mid-procedure causes stress. Setup everything (including the 'just in case' items) before the patient enters. Check your setup against the visual guide.

action_statement: I always ask the patient a curious open-ended question as I am seating them
description: Simple, curious questions help kids feel seen and ease into the visit. It turns the room into a friendlier place and helps you build trust early.
intervention_text: Distraction starts with connection. Ask about a pet, a sport, or a shoe color. Any topic other than teeth helps the child settle in.

action_statement: I always accurately enter patient's height and weight in the proper units and double check for errors before seating them.
description: Accurate measurements matter for safe dosing and charting. Double-checking helps you avoid mistakes and keeps the appointment on track.
intervention_text: Dosage depends on this. If the scale looks off, re-weigh them. Accuracy here prevents medication errors.

action_statement: I always notice and verbally affirm specific positive behaviors during clinical activities
intervention_text: Catch them being good. Don't wait for the end. Say Great job holding open every 60 seconds. It reinforces the behavior you want.

action_statement: When I notice that I’m starting an appointment more than 10 minutes late, I check with the Lead RDA before starting so that I understand the plan to get back on track.
description: Time warnings help you stay ahead of delays. Looping in the lead quickly keeps the day flowing and prevents small issues from becoming big bottlenecks.

action_statement: Before beginning a clinical activity I tell the patient that they can raise their hand to ask me to pause at any time
description: Giving kids permission to pause puts them back in control. It lowers fear, builds trust, and helps the whole visit feel more predictable.
intervention_text: Control reduces pain. Tell the child: Raise your left hand if you need a break. It makes them feel safe enough to cooperate.

action_statement: I always anticipate the next instrument the doctor will need and have it in hand before the doctor asks for it.
description: Smooth assisting feels almost choreographed. Anticipating the doctor’s needs creates a seamless experience for the patient and keeps procedures efficient.
intervention_text: Stay one step ahead. Watch the Doctor's eyes, not just their hands. If they look at the composite, have the curing light ready.

action_statement: When I have 45 minutes or more between patients I always use that time to send messages to the Reschedule list to help fill the schedule.
description: Small pockets of time add up. Using those moments to reach out to the Reschedule list keeps the day efficient and helps patients stay on track with needed care.

action_statement: After the doctor explains the treatment and leaves the chair, I always check for comprehension and clearly narrate next steps
description: When the doctor steps away, parents often still have questions. A quick, friendly recap ensures understanding and builds trust in the plan.
intervention_text: The unknown is scary. Tell them exactly what happens next: We go to the front, we sign one paper, and we book for Tuesday. Roadmap the exit.

action_statement: As the doctor calls out findings, I actively listen and accurately record correct conditions on correct teeth (both in note and charted on the odontogram)
description: Accurate charting helps the whole team deliver safe, consistent care. Listening closely and recording precisely avoids errors and protects the patient record.
intervention_text: Listen for the code. If the Doctor mumbles, ask them to repeat. Charting Watch vs Treat changes the entire treatment plan.

action_statement: After taking an x-ray I always label the teeth in the images before leaving the workstation
description: Labeling images immediately keeps records clear and helps the doctor diagnose without delay. It also prevents mix-ups later in the day.
intervention_text: Data without labels is useless. Tag the teeth numbers immediately after exposure. Unlabeled mounts confuse the whole clinical team.

action_statement: Except in extreme cases, I always request that all families leave us a Google review after their appointment, and direct them to the QR code to scan.
description: Google reviews are a huge part of families discovering our excellent care. We ask for them to help make sure other people can find us and get great oral healthcare.
intervention_text: Compliments don't count; reviews do. If they say You guys are great, reply: The best way to thank us is scanning this QR code.

action_statement: I always link the dentist’s recommended treatment to the parent's desired outcome for their child
description: Parents care most about the end result—linking the treatment to their goals helps everything make sense. When you make that connection clear, it builds trust and keeps the path forward focused on what matters to them.
intervention_text: Connect the dot to their goal. You said you wanted to avoid pain for him? This filling stops the pain before it starts.

action_statement: After restating critical feedback, I always use the phrase "tell me more" and actively listen to the response.
description: “Tell me more” opens the door for clarity. It signals that you’re not defending—you’re understanding. Active listening helps families feel heard and respected.
intervention_text: Curiosity cures conflict. If a parent is upset, lean in. Tell me more about that. Let them vent before you solve.

action_statement: When pulling up radiographs prior to doctor's arrival, I always highlight OVERJET, and explain the benefits to the patient.
description: By speaking confidently about the technology we use, it gives us credibility and authority.
intervention_text: We're a cutting edge practice. Highlight this to make that clear.

action_statement: When hesitation surfaces, I always identify the primary concern, comfort, time, or cost, so I can respond to the right thing.
description: You're likely the first person to hear about a worry. That means you're the most likely to understand exactly where it's coming from.
intervention_text: Don't be afraid to slow down, ask questions, and help the parent feel heard about whatever their concern is.

action_statement: I always write name, age, and any patient portion on the board after finishing check-in, and hand it directly to an available RDA.
description: Keep the board clean and color-coded, it’s how the team stays synced, we always hand it off to make sure that the back knows that a patient is ready.

action_statement: I always use the CareStack list function to identify and contact 10 patients per empty treatment slot.
description: Use your tools like a pro. Ten quick contacts can turn an empty slot into a full day and make your schedule much healthier.
intervention_text: Volume is the cure for empty chairs. Don't just call one; call ten. Use the Quick Fill list in CareStack to burn through numbers faster.

action_statement: As the doctor presents treatment options, I always actively listen, and accurately record all mutually agreed upon treatment.
description: Documenting agreed treatment clearly supports scheduling, billing, and follow-up care. Precise notes prevent confusion and keep the patient journey smooth.
intervention_text: Capture the agreement. If the parent agrees to the sealant but declines the fluoride, mark it immediately. Don't rely on memory.

action_statement: I always invite the guardian to share back the key parts of the post-op plan to confirm their understanding and comfort with next steps.
description: A brief teach-back helps you catch misunderstandings early. It makes parents feel supported while ensuring their child’s recovery stays on track.
intervention_text: Verify understanding. Ask: Just so I know I explained it right, what is the plan for dinner tonight? (Soft foods/etc).

action_statement: For all patients, I always verify that the adult with them is listed on the Authorized Individual Form before beginning the appointment
description: Checking authorization keeps every interaction safe and compliant. This quick verification protects patients, families, and the practice.
intervention_text: Protect the minor. If Grandma brings the child, check the Authorized list before you talk about medical history. HIPAA matters.

action_statement: I always transfer appointment related call summaries from VoiceStack into the patient memo.
description: Notes tell the story between calls and visits. Keep them updated so every teammate knows what’s already been said and what comes next.
intervention_text: If it's not in the note, it didn't happen. If you struggle to transfer notes, do it while you are on the phone, not after.

action_statement: I always complete all items in the VoiceStack "To-Do" list before the end of the day every day.
description: Finish what you start. A clear To-Do list means clean communication, no loose ends, and zero “Did anyone handle that?” moments.
intervention_text: Clear the deck. Leaving tasks for tomorrow creates a debt that slows you down. Knock out the 3 easiest tasks on your list right now.

action_statement: When I receive a same-day emergency call, I adjust schedules to accommodate, verify insurance if i can, and prepare patient to pay the 'Standard Limited Exam Fee' if I cannot.
description: Emergencies test your calm. Act fast, stay clear, and keep patients informed so the day stays under control, even when it’s not.
intervention_text: Empathy + Boundary. You can care about their pain while being firm about the fee. Ask a Lead to roleplay the Limited Exam Fee conversation with you.

action_statement: When I notice my own stress rising, I always pause for one deep breath to center myself before speaking or acting.
description: A quick reset protects the room from tension. One calm breath helps you show up with patience, clarity, and kindness—even in busy moments.
intervention_text: You can't pour from an empty cup. If you are frustrated, turn away for 3 seconds, breathe in for 4, out for 4. Reset before you re-engage.

action_statement: When cost is a concern, I explain that the doctor has prioritized what’s most important to do first but that we can plan the rest in safe stages. I communicate the worries with the treatment coordinator.
description: Cost worries are normal. Staying calm and explaining that the doctor has already prioritized the safest order helps families feel supported—not pressured. Handing off to the treatment coordinator keeps the conversation clear, kind, and organized.
intervention_text: Don't negotiate clinical need. Validate the cost, then hand off. I know it's an investment. Let's have the Treatment Coordinator see how to fit this into your budget.

action_statement: I always respond to cost concerns by higlighting all flexible payment options available.
description: When money comes up, people tense up. Your calm, confident tone, and a clear list of options, turns a hard moment into a trust moment.
intervention_text: Cost fear is real. Don't just list prices; offer solutions. Review the CareCredit and Payment Plan talking points today so you can offer them fluently.

action_statement: Even if confirmed, I always call all treatment visits for the following day, review NPO guidelines, and communicate the importance of their attendance.
description: A reminder call isn’t just logistics, it’s reassurance. It shows families you’re invested in their visit and that every appointment matters.
intervention_text: A confirmation call is a medical safety check. If you feel rushed, pause. This call prevents the Sorry, we can't treat you conversation tomorrow.

action_statement: When a patient is greater than 10 minutes late, i always communicate our understanding, then acknowledge that their wait may be more than usual.
description: Late arrivals happen, how you handle them matters. Be kind, stay direct, and reset expectations so the visit still feels organized and calm.
intervention_text: Resetting expectations saves the relationship. Don't just say Okay. Say: We'll squeeze you in, but there will be a wait. Be honest about the consequence.

action_statement: Before dismissal, I always ensure the next visit is scheduled at the clinically appropriate interval
description: Locking in the next visit keeps treatment on track. Making sure families know exactly who to reach out to prevents confusion and gives them a clear pathway for support.

action_statement: I always share a quick, positive story about how this treatment helped another child feel better or stay healthy (no names or details), so parents can picture the real benefit.
description: A short, anonymous success story helps parents imagine the positive outcome for their own child. It replaces fear with a clearer picture of what good care can do.
intervention_text: Social proof works. We had a kiddo just last week with this same issue, and they did great. Normalize the success.

action_statement: I always preview our use of OVERJET as the most 'advanced AI powered xray technology' when explaining the flow of a new patient visit.
description: When you talk about OVERJET, keep it simple and confident. It tells families your team uses the best tools for their child’s care, no tech talk required.
intervention_text: AI sounds scary; Precision sounds safe. Ask the Doctor to show you an OVERJET image so you can see exactly what you are describing to parents.

action_statement: For all new-patient booking calls, I direct the caller to their patient portal, and confirm they have been able to successfully log in before ending the call.
description: Before you hang up, make sure they can log in. One minute now saves five later and keeps paperwork from piling up at the front desk.

action_statement: I am able to summarize the basic steps for all common clinical procedures.
description: Know the flow before the patient sits down. Explaining procedures clearly builds confidence, yours and theirs.
intervention_text: Patients fear the unknown. If you can't explain a Pulpotomy simply, ask a Lead RDA to describe it to you in plain English today.

action_statement: Before lunch and at the end of the day, I always check high-turnover disposables and note anything running low so we never start short.
description: Quick supply checks prevent mid-day shortages. Catching low items early keeps procedures running smoothly and protects the pace of care.
intervention_text: No surprises. Check the high-volume items (suction tips, gauze) before the afternoon rush. Running out mid-procedure is preventable.

action_statement: I always monitor patient comfort, scanning for breathing, tension, and signs of anxiety, and narrate progress or use distraction to reduce stress, unless the doctor is already managing comfort, in which case I support their lead.
description: Comfort cues are easy to miss. Noticing a child’s breathing or body tension early lets you step in before anxiety builds. If the doctor’s already leading, your role is quiet support, matching tone and reinforcing calm.
intervention_text: You are the patient's advocate. Watch their hands. If they clench, touch their shoulder and remind them to breathe. Don't just watch the tooth.

action_statement: When the treatment coordinator is occupied I always step in and handle any payment of outstanding balance using the card reader
description: Step in when things jam. You’re not just helping with payments, you’re keeping the day from slowing down.
intervention_text: You are the backup engine. If the card reader intimidates you, grab a Lead right now and run a $1.00 test charge and refund. Muscle memory cures fear.

action_statement: I set aside time daily to call or text people on the "Incomplete Paperwork" list in order to keep same-day verifications below 3%
description: Keep paperwork from becoming panic work. A quick call or text today prevents tomorrow’s bottleneck.
intervention_text: Chasing forms is better than stalling the clinic. Send 3 texts right now to tomorrow's Incomplete list. Future-you will thank you.

action_statement: I always review the entire room reset checklist and confirm every item is complete before considering the room ready for the next patient.
description: A complete reset keeps every patient safe and every provider set up for success. Following the checklist ensures nothing gets missed and the room starts clean, stocked, and ready.
intervention_text: Don't trust your memory; trust the checklist. One missed item can delay the next appointment. Physically touch the checklist for your next turnover.

action_statement: I always make sure there are zero 'pending follow up' items inside the VoiceStack Opportunities tab by the end of the day
description: End every day clean. When follow-ups are handled, the system, and the team, runs smoother.
intervention_text: A clean dashboard is a clean mind. If Pending Follow-ups are piling up, ask the Office Manager to help you triage the list for 15 minutes today.

action_statement: When a clinical question is beyond my knowledge, I create and assign a 'To-Do' in VoiceStack (phone) or CareStack (in-person), and inform the patient that someone will reach out within 24 hrs.
description: You don’t need to know everything, you just need to close the loop. Logging a To-Do and setting clear follow-up expectations shows accuracy and accountability.
intervention_text: I don't know is a brave answer, as long as it's followed by I'll find out. Log the To-Do immediately. If you forget to log tasks, use a sticky note buffer.

action_statement: I always use the question "What are your goals for your child's oral health over the next 5 years?" during a new patient appointment.
description: Asking about goals shows the parent that their priorities matter. It gives the doctor helpful context and helps families feel like true partners in their child’s care.

action_statement: I always ask patients at least one curious, open-ended question during the check in process.
description: Curiosity creates connection. One sincere question can shift a rushed check-in into a real conversation.
intervention_text: Break the script. Ask one kid today: What was the best part of your weekend? Watch how it changes the energy of the check-in.

action_statement: I always check throughout the day to make sure the correct music is playing at an appropriate level
description: The sound of the office shapes how people feel. Keep it calm, friendly, and at a volume that lets conversation breathe.
intervention_text: Vibes matter. If the music is too loud or too sleepy, change it. You are the DJ of the patient experience.

action_statement: As part of the administrative team, I always dress in business casual attire when I am at work, even on non-patient days
description: The way you show up changes the energy of the whole office. Professional doesn’t mean fancy, it means showing pride in your work every day.
intervention_text: Your look signals authority. If you're unsure about an outfit, check the Culture Guide or simply ask a Lead DFI: Is this client-ready?

action_statement: When presented with critical feedback, I always ensure that a next-step or resolution has been found before finishing the interaction.
description: Don’t end a feedback talk without a plan. We don't want to walk away without knowing at least a next step, even if it's just coordinating a chat with a manager.
intervention_text: Don't let them leave angry. Before they go, ask: Do you feel like we have a plan to fix this? If they say no, get the Manager.

action_statement: Every day I pull the Same Day Verification report for the next 3 days and send it to Medusind
description: Staying ahead on insurance verification keeps appointments smooth and reduces day-of delays. A quick daily report ensures families are ready and the clinical team isn’t stuck waiting.
intervention_text: This prevents billing fires. If Medusind doesn't get this, we work for free. Make this the very first thing you do after logging in, even before checking email.

action_statement: I always state that fluoride will be done and note the uncovered fee, rather than asking permission, and I direct any follow-up questions to the clinical team.
description: Stating fluoride confidently helps avoid confusion and keeps the visit on track. You normalize the recommendation, explain the uncovered fee, and let the clinical team address any detailed questions.
intervention_text: Don't ask for permission; inform of the plan. Instead of Do you want fluoride?, say: We're applying the fluoride varnish today. Confidence prevents the objection.

action_statement: I always use fresh cleaning rags for each individual patient encounter
description: Using a new rag for every patient protects against cross-contamination and keeps the room visibly clean. It’s a small step that makes a big difference in safety.
intervention_text: Visibility is trust. If a parent sees a used rag, they doubt the sterile instruments. Use a fresh rag for every single patient, no exceptions.

action_statement: I always offer parents a coffee and patients a blanket prior to all procedures.
description: Small gestures make big impressions. Offering comfort items helps families relax and shows that you’re thinking about their experience, not just the procedure.
intervention_text: Comfort comes first. Before you lean the chair back, offer a blanket. It takes 10 seconds and buys you 10 minutes of cooperation.

action_statement: I always set patients up for comfort by offering a headset and asking them what they'd like to watch.
description: Helping the patient choose something to watch gives them control and distraction during the visit. It turns an unfamiliar procedure into something familiar and safe.
intervention_text: Give them control. Letting the child pick the show gives them agency in a scary environment. Do this before you open any instruments.

action_statement: After each applicable procedure, I always attach one intraoral photo to support patient understanding and insurance documentation.
description: A clear photo helps parents understand the procedure and strengthens documentation for the doctor and insurance. It’s a quick step that adds clarity for everyone.
intervention_text: A picture justifies the claim. If you struggle to get good angles, grab a Lead RDA between patients and practice your camera positioning.

action_statement: I always complete and save clinical notes as a draft before the end of each appointment.
description: Complete notes keep the entire care team aligned. Finishing them before the appointment ends ensures accuracy and prevents details from being forgotten.
intervention_text: Notes are legal documents. Don't wait until lunch. Finish the draft before you dismiss the patient, while the details are fresh.

action_statement: When the doctor enters, I always present the patient by name, state the planned procedure, share relevant medical history, and relay any parent questions or concerns.
description: A smooth handoff helps the doctor focus immediately and shows the family that you’re all on the same page. Presenting the patient clearly builds trust and keeps the visit efficient.
intervention_text: Summarize to build trust. State the plan clearly in front of the parent: This is [Name], we are doing [Procedure]. It shows the team is aligned.

action_statement: I always play the correct Parent Pre-Treatment video prior to Dr. arrival in the room
description: This video helps make sure parents understand their role is during the treatment, and helps prevent interruptions as much as possible.
intervention_text: Let the screen do the teaching. Playing the video ensures the parent gets the standard info while you set up the tray.

action_statement: I’m always prepared to perform any maintenance or compliance task listed in the Uptime checklist when assigned.
description: Staying ready for maintenance tasks keeps the office safe and compliant. Following the checklist consistently supports the entire team’s workflow.
intervention_text: Consistency is safety. Don't skip the boring checks. Verify the O2 tank or the autoclave logs. It matters.

action_statement: I always actively manage doctor flow by clearly communicating when and where patients are ready, including location, procedure, and patient type, to keep the schedule running smoothly.
description: Clear, proactive updates keep the doctor moving efficiently. Sharing the right details at the right moment prevents confusion and helps the entire day run smoothly.
intervention_text: Be the traffic controller. Tell the doctor exactly where to go next. Room 2 is ready for numbing. Direct traffic to save time.

action_statement: I always maintain the same professional pace and focus whether the office is calm or hectic.
description: A steady pace builds trust with both patients and the team. Staying consistent—even when things get busy—helps the day feel organized instead of chaotic.
intervention_text: Calm adds speed. Rushing creates mistakes. Take one deep breath. Move with purpose, not panic. The patient mirrors your energy.

action_statement: I always communicate the importance of X-rays to our standard of care any time a parent objects or attempts to decline them.
description: X-rays help the doctor catch things we can’t see with our eyes. Explaining that clearly—and kindly—helps parents understand that imaging isn’t optional; it’s part of providing complete and safe care.
intervention_text: To see is to know. Explain: We can't fix what we can't see. The X-ray ensures we don't miss a cavity hiding in between.

action_statement: When presented with critical feedback or conflict from a parent or guardian, I always ensure that a next-step or resolution has been found before finishing the interaction.
description: Every piece of feedback needs a clear finish. Ending with a concrete next step shows professionalism and turns criticism into forward motion.

action_statement: I always center myself and smile in real life before answering the phone, ensuring a warm tone of voice.
description: Families can hear your smile. Taking a breath before answering helps you sound warm and steady, turning every phone call into a positive first impression.
intervention_text: You can hear a smile. If you're stressed, the caller hears Busy. Take one breath, physically smile, then pick up. It hacks your brain into warmth.

action_statement: When I am on the phone and a patient walks in, I find the soonest natural break and kindly place them on a brief hold in order to serve the patient in front of me.
description: Balancing in-person and phone communication takes awareness. Stepping away at a natural pause lets you greet walk-ins warmly without leaving your caller hanging. Both patients feel seen, not sidelined.
intervention_text: The person in front of you wins. It feels rude to interrupt the caller, but it's worse to ignore the lobby. Practice the phrase: I have a patient walking in, may I place you on a brief hold?

action_statement: I always check the voicemails / missed calls on Voicestack in the AM, at lunch, and in the PM and take action as necessary.
description: Checking missed calls throughout the day keeps communication tight and prevents families from feeling ignored. A quick sweep in the morning, at lunch, and before closing helps make sure no one slips through the cracks.
intervention_text: The AM/Lunch/PM rhythm is non-negotiable. If you skip the Lunch check, the PM pile becomes unmanageable. Set a phone alarm for just before Lunch to clear the board.

action_statement: Every Monday I use Carestack to pull the 'Interpreter Report'  for the next 2 weeks and schedule interpreters as necessary.
description: Planning interpreters ahead of time removes stress for families and the clinical team. A quick Monday check ensures every patient feels supported and nothing gets missed at the last minute.
intervention_text: Monday automation sets up the week. If you forget this, we scramble later. If necessary, set a recurring reminder on your phone for Interpreter Audit at 9:00 AM on Mondays right now.

action_statement: Every Monday I pull the missing codes report for the next 3 months and fill in all missing codes
description: Filling in missing codes early keeps schedules accurate and prevents last-minute surprises. A weekly sweep ensures records are complete and billing runs smoothly.
intervention_text: Missing codes mean missing revenue. If scanning 3 months feels overwhelming, break it down. Do Next Month today, and the rest tomorrow. Just get started.

action_statement: I always remind patients to access and complete the patient portal prior to arrival, and warn about delays if they do not
description: A gentle reminder about the portal helps families come prepared and keeps their visit running smoothly. Setting expectations early prevents delays and shows that you’re looking out for their time.
intervention_text: The warning isn't a threat; it's a kindness. If you don't warn them about the delay, they will blame you when they have to wait. Say: To keep your appointment time protected, we need this done now.

action_statement: I always apply the Alcan template to write a personalized response to all positive Google reviews within 24 hrs.
description: Responding to positive reviews quickly shows gratitude and strengthens relationships. Personalizing each message makes families feel recognized and reinforces what they loved about their visit.
intervention_text: Speed matters. A response 3 days later looks automated. Copy the Alcan Template to a sticky note on your desktop so you can paste-and-personalize in 30 seconds.

action_statement: I always schedule the 6-month recare apppointment while the patient is in-chair
description: Keeping our patients in a consistent flow is crucial, and you're in the best position to make sure this gets done every time.
intervention_text: Don't rely on the front desk. The best time to rebook is when the patient is happy in the chair. Say: Let's secure your spot for 6 months so you get the time you want.

action_statement: Before treatment begins, I always preview the doctor, the procedure, and invite any questions or concerns from the parent or patient.
description: Kids relax when they know what’s about to happen, and parents trust you when you take time to include them. A calm preview sets the tone, everyone understands what’s next, and the doctor walks into a prepared, confident room.
intervention_text: By providing a clear description of what's next, you give patient and parent a chance to calm, and to get a pulse check that you can relay to the doctor.

action_statement: I always use "estimated insurance benefits/ savings" and "patient portion/ responsibility" instead of "covered/not covered" and "out-of-pocket".
description: We always refer to insurance as a benefit or a savings so there's less surprise when treatment isn't fully covered. "Out-of-pocket" gives families the mental image that we’re “reaching into their pocket” for money.

action_statement: I always use "estimated insurance benefits/ savings" and "patient portion/ responsibility" instead of "covered/not covered" and "out-of-pocket".
description: We always refer to insurance as a benefit or a savings so there's less surprise when treatment isn't fully covered. "Out-of-pocket" gives families the mental image that we’re “reaching into their pocket” for money.
intervention_text: Our language sets the tone. Try to catch yourself using these phrases and eliminate them from your work vocabulary.

action_statement: When discussing Zirconia crowns with a guardian, I always communicate their value by highlighting that we're unique in placing them, their improved appearance, and their long term durability.
description: We believe in this treatment, even if insurers don't. So we need to be able to explain why, and why the family should care.

action_statement: I always begin my check in process by confirming the preferred name and relationship for the person who has brought the patient (i.e mom, aunt, grandma), and checking to ensure they are authorized.
description: This first matters for HIPAA compliance, but also because it's valuable for us to know exactly what folks like to be called!
intervention_text: Don't forget this, it's CRUCIAL that we make sure patients are with someone approved to bring them in for treatment. It never hurts to ask!

action_statement: I always verify team attendance for both ProMove meetings each week and follow up with any team member who misses one within one business day.
description: Ensuring consistent attendance at ProMove meetings keeps everyone aligned on priorities and learning, and prevents the same people from repeatedly missing key development time.
resources_url: Block time each week to check attendance right after meetings and send quick follow-ups to anyone who missed.

action_statement: I always schedule time each week to observe the RDA to Doctor hand-off, document at least one opportunity for improvement, and follow up with the appropriate team member about it.
description: Regularly observing clinical hand-offs helps catch small communication gaps before they become bigger patient experience or clinical quality issues.
resources_url: Put a recurring weekly calendar block to shadow hand-offs and write down at least one concrete improvement to discuss.

action_statement: Each week, I review all Uptime tasks related to clinical equipment with my Lead RDA and ensure every item is either completed or has a clear due date before the end of that week.
description: Reviewing Uptime tasks weekly keeps clinical equipment safe, compliant, and ready, reducing the risk of breakdowns and safety incidents.
resources_url: Set a standing weekly meeting with your Lead RDA to review Uptime tasks together and close any open items.

action_statement: I always review last week’s key KPIs every Monday (i.e production, collections, Google Reviews, and New Patient #’s), identify problem areas, and send my Regional Manager an action plan to address.
description: A weekly KPI review with an action plan keeps the practice focused on the numbers that matter and turns issues into concrete steps, not just awareness.
resources_url: Protect time every Monday to review KPIs and send a short, specific action plan email to your Regional Manager.

action_statement: I always take action on every item in the the Voicestack “Potential Opportunities” column before the end of the day.
description: Acting on Voicestack opportunities daily prevents missed treatment, callbacks, and follow-ups that would otherwise leak revenue and hurt patient experience.
resources_url: Schedule a short block near the end of each day to clear or assign every “Potential Opportunities” item.

action_statement: I always ensure the phone is answered by either me or a team member within 3 rings
description: Holding the team to a three-ring standard reduces missed calls and gives parents confidence that the office is responsive and organized.
resources_url: Review call reports regularly and coach team members when the three-ring standard isn’t being met.

action_statement: I always ensure that all appointments scheduled within the next 48 hours have a documented confirmation (call, text, or email) by either myself or my team.
description: Confirming upcoming appointments 48 hours in advance reduces no-shows and last-minute gaps that hurt production and flow.
resources_url: Build a daily 48-hour confirmation routine and check the report until it’s consistently at 100%.

action_statement: I always review the schedule 48 hours in advance and ensure families missing paperwork are contacted with clear instructions by either myself or my team.
description: Catching missing paperwork ahead of time prevents bottlenecks at check-in and helps the day start smoothly for both staff and families.
resources_url: Add a 48-hour paperwork review to your daily schedule and verify that every family has been contacted.

action_statement: I always review Iris chats at the end of each day and ensure all messages are responded to or assigned to a specific owner by either myself or my team.
description: Closing out Iris chats daily keeps digital communication tight and prevents parent messages from slipping through the cracks.
resources_url: Before leaving, open Iris and make sure every chat is either answered or clearly assigned.

action_statement: I always check for and ensure a response to all online appointment requests every day.
description: Responding to online appointment requests daily shows parents you are responsive and prevents missed opportunities to fill the schedule.
resources_url: Set a daily reminder to check online requests and make sure each one is scheduled, declined with a note, or set for follow-up.

action_statement: I always analyze common claim flags at least once a week and communicate specific behavior changes to the team during huddle, then monitor whether those flags decrease over time.
description: Looking at patterns in claim flags and changing behavior prevents the same billing mistakes from happening over and over again.
resources_url: Choose one or two recurring flag types each week, share the “why” in huddle, and track if those flags drop.

action_statement: I always review all uncollected balances two business days before the scheduled appointment
description: Reviewing uncollected balances ahead of visits allows you to plan for conversations and avoid surprises at the front desk.
resources_url: Use a 2-day-ahead report to flag uncollected balances and note how each account will be handled at the visit.

action_statement: I always ensure families with uncollected balances are contacted by phone or text prior to their appointment to review payment expectations or arrangements.
description: Proactively contacting families about balances reduces awkward day-of conversations and improves the chance you’ll collect what is owed.
resources_url: Make it a habit to reach out early about balances so families know what to expect before they arrive.

action_statement: I always complete and submit the Daily Production Report and verify it matches production figures in Carestack before 10am the following day.
description: Completing and reconciling the Daily Production Report keeps your numbers accurate and builds trust in the practice’s reporting.
resources_url: Block time each morning to finish the DPR and double-check it against Carestack before 10am.

action_statement: I always review claim flags daily and work or assign them so that unactioned flags remain below 10.
description: Keeping claim flags low ensures claims move quickly, reducing delays in payment and preventing growing backlogs.
resources_url: Check claim flags every day and don’t let the unactioned count creep above 10.

action_statement: I always walk the floor twice daily to check in briefly with every team member, address any immediate barriers, and give specific encouragement when I see something done well.
description: Being visibly present and supportive on the floor builds morale, surfaces issues early, and reinforces positive behaviors in real time.
resources_url: Set two daily reminders to step out of your office, walk the floor, and connect with each team member.

action_statement: I always personally follow up with any parent concern or complaint escalated to me before the end of the next day, clearly summarizing what we’ll do next and how they can reach me if necessary
description: Prompt, personal follow-up on escalated concerns shows parents that their experience matters and helps rebuild trust after a problem.
resources_url: When a concern is escalated, note it immediately and schedule time to call or speak with that parent before the next day ends.

action_statement: I always stay aware of the overall mood in the office throughout the day, I pause what I’m doing as necessary to either reset the tone with encouragement and clarity or address the source of tension directly with the team.
description: Managing the overall mood in the office keeps stress from spreading and helps the team stay calm, focused, and patient-centered.
resources_url: When you feel the energy dip or spike, take a moment to name it, reset expectations, and offer calm, clear guidance.

action_statement: I always confirm that our assigned social media content for the week (photos, videos, or stories) has been gathered from the team and submitted to the marketing contact by the end of the last clinic day of the week.
description: Consistently submitting social content keeps your community presence active and shows families what makes your practice special.
resources_url: Choose a specific day each week to collect content from the team and send it to marketing before the day ends.

action_statement: I always use the language ‘estimated insurance benefits’ and ‘estimated family contribution,’ and I never use the words ‘covered’ or ‘out-of-pocket’ when discussing costs with parents.
description: Using precise, consistent language about costs reduces confusion and prevents parents from feeling misled about what insurance will pay.
resources_url: Practice this phrasing before case presentations so it becomes automatic in every money conversation.

action_statement: I always respond to financial concerns with a clear explanation of all options including reasonably breaking up treatment and using CareCredit
description: Offering clear, flexible payment options helps parents say yes to needed treatment without feeling pressured or stuck.
resources_url: When a parent hesitates over cost, slow down and walk through each payment option calmly and clearly.

action_statement: I always review and submit all preauthorization documentation no more than 48 hours after treatment acceptance.
description: Submitting preauthorizations within 48 hours speeds up insurance decisions and keeps treatment moving forward without long delays.
resources_url: After a case is accepted, make it a rule to start and finish preauths within the next two working days.

action_statement: I always review preauthorization approvals every day and follow up with insurance as necssary.
description: Checking preauth approvals daily ensures you don’t miss a green light from insurance or let stalled cases sit without action.
resources_url: Add preauth approvals to your daily checklist and follow up on anything pending or unclear.

action_statement: I always personally complete the full check-in process with at least one family each day, modeling over-the-top hospitality by greeting them by name, confirming comfort, offering amenities, and setting clear expectations for the visit so the team sees the standard we expect.
description: Personally modeling exceptional hospitality sets the tone for the whole team and shows exactly what a 5-star check-in should look and feel like.
resources_url: Choose one family each day to check in yourself and use that moment to model the warmth and clarity you expect from the team.

action_statement: I always verbalize the exam findings in it's entirety to the RDA/AI- including: extraoral findings, TMJ, intraoral soft tissue findings, current dentition, hard tissue findings, radiographic findings, occlusion, and airway.
description:
Using a consistent verbal exam sequence ensures that every critical part of the evaluation is completed and documented, reducing the risk that important findings are missed.

Speaking findings clearly and in the same order each time allows the RDA and AI documentation tools to accurately capture the exam, improving charting quality and reducing the need for corrections after the visit.

action_statement: I always check to confirm parent alignment with the mutually agreed upon treatment recommendation before leaving the room- directly asking them "how are you feeling about the plan as it stands?"
description: After reviewing treatment recommendations, I pause to check how the parent is feeling about the plan to ensure they feel heard and comfortable moving forward. This brief alignment check reinforces shared decision-making, builds trust, and helps prevent confusion or hesitation about next steps.

action_statement: I always offer and consider general anesthesia as a treatment modality for extensive treatment needs (3+ quads) children with behavioral concerns, or medically complex children who are high risk candidates and not suitable for oral sedation, or based on parent preference for GA.
description: For children requiring extensive treatment, pre-cooperative patients, or those with special healthcare needs, I consider general anesthesia as a safe and predictable option to complete care comfortably and effectively. Recommending GA when appropriate helps prevent traumatic or failed sedation attempts and allows comprehensive treatment to be completed efficiently in a controlled environment.

action_statement: I always look for opportunities to consolidate treatment into fewer visits, so families save trips, time out of school, and repeat sedation events.
description: Consolidating care reduces the financial, emotional, and logistical burden of repeat visits for families, and improves chair utilization for the practice.

action_statement: I always offer same day sealants, hall crowns, and space maintainers - and always consider other same day restorative treatment when the schedule permits.
description: When clinically appropriate and the schedule allows, I offer same-day treatment opportunities to reduce unnecessary return visits for families. Addressing small or preventive needs during the same appointment improves convenience for parents, strengthens patient satisfaction, and makes better use of available chair time.

action_statement: I always use authentic conversation and storytelling with relatable examples to build trust with patients and parents.
description:
At every patient interaction, I strive to communicate in a way that feels human, relatable, and authentic, using clear explanations, conversational language, and appropriate storytelling to help families understand their child’s oral health.

Rather than delivering information in a purely clinical or transactional way, I aim to create a comfortable dialogue that builds trust and connection.

action_statement: After treatment I always share clear instructions and set expectations for patients and parents about numbness, food/drink to avoid, and reasons to call in case of concern.
description: You are the conductor, even though the doctor performs the procedure, it's your patient. You make sure that the parents and patients understand what they need to in order to have the best post-op experience possible
intervention_text: This is really important! Go ahead and find someone to practice this with.

action_statement: I always recommend a crown as the treatment option with the highest long-term success rate for primary tooth lesions that are structurally high-risk—specifically MO lesions on first primary molars, MOD lesions on any molar, lesions more than 50% into dentin, anterior lesions involving 3 or more surfaces or the incisal edge, and lesions of any size in a child being treated under general anesthesia.
I treatment plan anterior teeth under general anesthesia with heightened caution and transparency, recommending zirconia crowns for restorable teeth or extraction when prognosis is poor.
I always focus on diagnosing and recommending the best treatment plan for the child, and I defer detailed financial coordination to the practice’s administrative team.
I always ensure that all procedures requiring special consent have the correct consent form completed, signed, and documented in the patient chart before treatment begins.
I always review our parental separation policy for oral sedation and general anesthesia during the treatment planning appointment so parents are not surprised on the day of treatment.

When a family travels a long distance to reach us or comes through a charitable care program, I always treatment plan definitively rather than watch-and-wait, so essential care is completed in as few visits as possible.
I always include an indirect pulp cap (IPC) in the treatment plan when a lesion approximates the pulp and pulp protection may be needed.
I always adhere to the AAPD Maximum Recommended Dose (MRD) and weight-based dosing guidelines for all oral sedation medications and never exceed these limits.
I always observe each of my staff members during procedures once a month, and deliver positive and constructive feedback as appropriate.
I always verbally dictate to RDA/AI a clear and accurate baseline oral health status at new patient exams- current teeth present, existing treatment, and any findings present.
description: At new patient exams, I verbally call out existing restorations, missing teeth, and prior treatment so the RDA and AI can accurately document the patient’s starting dentition. Establishing a clear baseline ensures diagnostic accuracy, protects the practice from confusion or liability later, and creates a reliable record for future care.

action_statement: I always update the odontogram and any clinical findings by verbally dictating them to the RDA/AI at each patient encounter.
description: At every exam, I verbally call out erupted, exfoliated, restored, or missing teeth so the RDA and AI can update the odontogram in real time. Keeping the odontogram current ensures the chart accurately reflects the patient’s dentition, improving diagnostic clarity, treatment planning, and continuity of care.

action_statement: I always verbalize to the RDA/AI to chart any incipient lesions so that preventative care can be offered or teeth can be appropriately monitored radiographically.
description: During exams, I verbally identify incipient enamel lesions so the RDA and AI can accurately document them in the chart. Clearly charting early caries supports preventive treatment, improves monitoring over time, and ensures early disease is not overlooked or minimized.

action_statement: I always explain cavities clearly- indicating to the parent there is a cavity in the first, second or third layer of tooth- instead of saying there is a "spot" "watch" or other minimizing language.
description: Minimizing language can lead to misunderstanding, delayed care, and erosion of trust. Clear language supports informed decision-making.

action_statement: I always offer sealants on healthy posterior primary and permanent teeth, regardless of insurance coverage.
description: Sealants significantly reduce caries risk. Families deserve to know preventive options even if insurance does not cover them.

action_statement: I always offer SDF (primary teeth) or Curodont (Permanent teeth) for incipient lesions.
description: Minimally invasive options allow early intervention and avoid progression.

action_statement: I always chart an appropriate caries risk assessment for every patient.
description: Caries risk determines radiograph frequency, preventive strategies, and recall intervals.

action_statement: I always ensure bitewings and any necessary PA's are taken every 6 months for patients with incipient lesions, history of caries or treatment in last 2 years, history of dental trauma, pulp therapy or other indications that would make them high caries risk or require more frequent follow up.
description: Higher-risk patients require more frequent and targeted imaging to avoid missed disease.

action_statement: I always instruct RDAs to take PAs for any teeth planned for extraction or pulp therapy, or with caries approaching the pulp.
description: PAs are essential for accurate diagnosis and informed consent prior to more invasive treatment.

action_statement: I always perform a comprehensive evaluation and full series of high-quality radiographs for new patient limited, or referral exams.
description: Limited exams for new patients often underrepresent disease. High-quality in-house imaging is necessary for accurate diagnosis.

action_statement: I always recommend a pano at new patient exams (around age 6–7+) and every three years thereafter, regardless of insurance coverage.
description: Panoramic imaging tracks growth, development, missing teeth, and pathology.

action_statement: I always offer definitive restorative treatment (composite, crown, EXT) for lesions extending past the DEJ.
description: Once decay has progressed into dentin, monitoring alone is no longer appropriate. Definitive treatment is the standard of care.

action_statement: I always offer both white and silver crown options when full-coverage restorations are indicated.
description: Families value choice and transparency on esthetics, durability, and outcomes. Equitable care means ensuring all families are informed of all options.

action_statement: When a primary molar is extracted or planned for extraction, I always evaluate whether space maintenance is indicated based on the patient's age, dental development, eruption status, and clinical circumstances, and document the decision and family discussion when applicable.
description: Premature tooth loss can affect eruption and alignment. Space maintainers help prevent bigger issues down the road.

action_statement: I always evaluate the need for an ortho referral around 7-8 and again around 12-13 - and an oral surgery referral for 3rds around 15-16
description: Early evaluation allows proactive planning and prevention of more complex issues.

action_statement: I always sign my clinical notes at the chair before the patient leaves.
description: Timely documentation ensures accuracy, prevents backlogs, and protects clinical integrity.

action_statement: I always send patient referrals at the chair before the patient leaves.
description: Immediate referrals reduce delays, confusion, and follow-up failures.

action_statement: I always print prescriptions at the chair before the patient leaves.
description: This prevents missed medications and unnecessary callbacks.

action_statement: I always complete sedation medication logs at the time of sedation.
description: Real-time documentation is critical for safety, compliance, and auditing.

action_statement: I Always Complete Team and Administrative Requests Within 24 Hours
description:
I complete email- or staff-requested tasks—such as insurance narratives, 22-point sheets, parent follow-ups, or other documentation requests—within 24 hours.

Whenever possible, I aim for same-day completion so the team can continue moving patient care and scheduling forward without delay.

action_statement: I always review radiographs using the AI overlay to ensure nothing is overlooked.
description: AI supports diagnostic accuracy and consistency, especially in complex cases.

action_statement: I always show up on time, prepared, and positive for morning huddle
description:
I arrive on time for morning huddle, attend consistently, and participate in a way that supports team alignment and a positive start to the day.

Morning huddle is an opportunity to lead through presence, preparedness, and constructive engagement, helping the team anticipate the day’s needs and maintain strong workflow.

action_statement: I always consider the trust impact on patients and my team when deciding to call in absent to work.
description: Absences affect patients, schedules, and team morale. Reliability is a leadership expectation.

action_statement: I Always Give and Receive Feedback with Respect
description: Feedback is part of working as a team. The goal is always to help each other do our jobs well and keep the day running smoothly, while maintaining trust and respect.

action_statement: I always allow RDAs to guide the flow of the day.
description:
I allow RDAs to guide the flow of the day and direct me to the next patient, trusting them to manage timing, readiness, and transitions between patients.

This allows every team member to focus on their role and do their job well.

action_statement: I always allow the RDA to formally present the patient and guardian to me before diving into the exam/treatment
description:
I pause and allow the RDA to formally present the patient and guardian at the chair for both new patient and recall exams before beginning my evaluation.

The RDA presentation provides the key clinical details so we can move smoothly from room to room while staying aligned as a team.

action_statement: I always trust the RDA to provide clear and appropriate post-operative instructions.
description: RDAs are trained to deliver routine post-op instructions consistently. Delegating allows doctors to focus on reassurance and next steps.

action_statement: I Always Warmly Greet the Family and Introduce Myself by Name
description:
I always pause, make eye contact, warmly greet the child and parent, and introduce myself by name when entering the room, especially when meeting a family for the first time.

I also acknowledge and thank the RDA for the introduction to reinforce teamwork in front of the family.

action_statement: I Always Project a Calm and Confident Presence
description: Parents and children often mirror the doctor emotional state. Calm, aligned presence supports comprehension and trust.

action_statement: I Always Ask “Tell Me More” When a Parent Hesitates on Treatment
description:
When a parent hesitates or declines recommended treatment, I begin the conversation with curiosity and listening, seeking to understand their concerns before responding.

If concerns persist after discussion, I clearly explain our standards of care and clinical recommendations, and establish clear, respectful boundaries when a parent’s requests for care repeatedly fall outside those standards.

action_statement: I always promptly loop in my office manager, regional manager, or clinical director when a team member or system issue prevents me from practicing according to our standards of care.
